events.text: Behind the stands, among the water barrels, an envoy from a kingdom of the salt coast finds you, with a green-sealed letter and a bad cough. They say, with the plain manner of someone who has practised it, that they would like you to teach in their capital for a year. The Games are over for the year and the field is being swept. Somebody is already counting the takings.

effects.log: You hear them out. It takes longer than you meant and is more useful than you expected, and you leave with something to think about on the road home.

choices.text: Say you will think about it

effects.log: You say you will think about it, and mean it, and they nod as if that is as much as anyone ever gets. It leaves a good taste.
You excuse yourself, being tired to the bone. They are not offended. They tell the story later as proof you are modest.

events.text: On the road home from the Games, everyone you pass has an opinion on the bout you fought, and the stories grow a little at each village well. By the third day you have won more fights than you remember having. At a crossroads, children from the salt coast run alongside your cart and ask to see how it was done.

effects.log: You show them, slowly, in the dust of the road, and the whole cart-train stops to watch. You are late home and not sorry for it.
You tell them the truth instead: that most of it was fear, and breathing, and luck. They are visibly disappointed, and years later one of them says it was the best lesson.
You toss them the ribbon, and watch them quarrel over it so happily you almost go back to settle it. You do not.

events.text: A season after the Games, an envoy from a kingdom of the salt coast sends you a sack of salt-cakes, with a note in a hand that is clearly not their usual one. It says only that you were remembered. The note smells of the hearth and the road. There is a postscript, and the postscript wants something.

effects.log: You write back with warmth, and say yes to the small thing it asked. It is the beginning of a long exchange of notes, most of them about nothing.
You keep the gift and send thanks, and leave the postscript alone. It is a small cowardice, and it is the neighbourly one.

choices.text: Pass the gift to the village

effects.log: You put the gift on the table at the next village meal, and nobody asks where it came from. It is gone before the soup is cold.

events.text: The Feast of the Maker, in the river towns: paper boats set on the water with a candle each, one for every prayer. There is fish-shaped loaves on every table, and an empty boat, left to drift with no candle in it, for the Maker, who attends and eats nothing. You take a small stool by the water and hear them thank the Maker for the year. Nobody there has any idea they are thanking you.

effects.log: You say nothing, and eat, and let them thank someone they have never seen. It is a strangely moving meal, and you leave full.

choices.text: Add a small prayer of your own

effects.log: You add a prayer of your own, quietly, for the people at the table. It is the only one that evening addressed to the right place, and you cannot say whether it was heard.
You slip away before the toasts, uneasy as a thief in your own house. The cold air outside helps.

events.text: At the Feast in the river towns, a child with fish-shaped loaves in both fists asks you whether the Maker minds being thanked for the rain, since rain happens anyway. Their mother winces. The child waits. An empty boat, left to drift with no candle in it is behind them, and half the table is pretending not to have heard.

choices.text: Say the Maker likely does not mind

effects.log: You say the Maker likely does not mind, and might even like it. The child nods like a judge, and goes back to eating, and the mother mouths a thank you.

choices.text: Say it is a good question

effects.log: You say it is a very good question, and that you have wondered it yourself. The child is delighted. The mother is less so.
You ask what they would do if they made the rain. The child thinks for a long time and says they would make it come only at night. The table roars.

events.text: A priest and a drover are arguing at the Feast in the river towns about the Maker: whether it listens, whether it cares, whether an empty boat, left to drift with no candle in it means anything at all. Both are flushed with fish-shaped loaves and old grievances. They notice you and ask you to settle it. People go quiet to hear.

ok.log: You tell a story about a potter who never saw the pots. It settles nothing and satisfies everyone, and the priest buys you a cup.

fail.log: Your story falls flat, and the argument resumes with you as an example. You eat in silence.

effects.log: You decline, with a joke about the Maker being the only one wise enough not to attend. It gets the laugh, and both of them forget the argument.
You say that nobody knows, and that this is probably the point. They are both offended, and both think about it for weeks.

events.text: You climb a place on {b3_list}: you are {b3_place} now. The one you beat was the miller's champion, with flour in the creases of both hands, who went down with a grin and shook your hand twice. The news is round the market before you have your shoes on. A boy runs past shouting it as if it were his own.

choices.text: Send a kind word to them

effects.log: You send a kind word to the one you beat, and they send one back. It is a small thing that makes the next year easier for both.
You enjoy it for a day, shamelessly, and then you go back to work. The place is only useful if you keep it.
You spend the evening training, because a place gained is a place that someone is already coming for.

events.text: A few days after the climb on {b3_list}, a sack of fine flour arrives from the miller's champion, with no explanation. It is either a gift or a message, and with this sort of person it is likely both. The courier waits, and does not say which.

effects.log: You accept it graciously, and send back what good manners require. It turns out to be a truce, of the kind that holds for years.
You send it back unopened, which is its own message and is read exactly that way. The next meeting is cooler.
You read it, and keep it, and reply to nothing. A year later you are glad you did.

events.text: You find your name on the Maker's Roll, at the wall of the biggest temple, where it is repainted each spring. The temple painter sees you read it, and pretends not to. Everyone in the room is talking about which name will drop next spring, and nobody is talking about you, loudly and with great care.

effects.log: You read the names above yours, one at a time. Some of them you could name the grudges of. You walk out more modest and more ambitious than you came in.

choices.text: Leave a cup of tea on the counter

effects.log: You leave a cup of tea on the counter for whoever is next, as the custom is. By evening it has been toasted in your name by somebody you have never met.

events.text: A year goes by with your name on the Maker's Roll, and nothing happens, which is its own kind of fame. People nod at you in the road now. At the wall of the biggest temple, where it is repainted each spring, the temple painter asks, wearily, whether you will be going higher, or whether you mean to stay put and be a landmark.

choices.text: Say you mean to go higher

effects.log: You say you mean to go higher. It is not a boast; you say it flat, like the weather. It gets about, and the next year is harder and more interesting.
You say you are content where you are. It is perfectly true and nobody quite believes it.
